messages.text: hi, my husband and I have two kids (8 and 5). can we get food stamps? money is tight

Hi! Yes, your family might be able to get food assistance (SNAP). I need a few details to check. Your household looks like 4 people: you, your husband, and your two kids.

1. How much does each of you earn **before taxes**, and how often are you paid (weekly, every two weeks, or monthly)?
2. Do you get any other income, like Social Security, unemployment, or child support?

I'll ask about rent and bills next.

I'm the one who's 35. My husband's 33. I work part-time and make $1,500 a month before taxes, paid monthly. My husband doesn't work. He gets $550 a month in Social Security survivor benefits. No other income. Kids are 8 and 5.

Thank you, that helps. Next:

1. How much do you pay each month for rent or a mortgage? Do you also pay separately for heating or cooling (like an electric or gas bill)?
2. Do you pay for child care so you can work? If so, about how much a month?
Rent is $700 a month and that includes all utilities, so we don't pay anything separately for heat or electric. And yes, we pay $362 a month for after-school care so I can work.

**Your family looks likely to get food assistance (SNAP).** My rough estimate is about **$700 a month**. That is only an estimate. Only the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS) decides.

**How I got there (household of 4)**
- **Your income before taxes:** $1,500 (your pay) + $550 (your husband's Social Security survivor benefits) = **$2,050 a month**.
- **Income limit:** For a family of four, the limit before deductions is **$3,575 a month** starting October 1, 2026 ([Colorado Politics, on USDA's 2026-27 numbers](https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/09/28/what-to-know-about-snap-increases-starting-oct-1-5/)). You are well under it.
- **Deductions:**
  - 20% of your wages ($300).
  - A standard deduction of about $220 to $230.
  - Your $362 in after-school care.
  - Part of your rent, about $118. Your rent counts, but since utilities are included, you get no separate utility deduction.
- **Income left after deductions:** about $1,050. The net limit for four people is $2,750 ([Colorado Politics](https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/09/28/what-to-know-about-snap-increases-starting-oct-1-5/)), so you are under it too.
- **Estimated benefit:** The most a family of four can get is **$1,023 a month** ([Colorado Politics](https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/09/28/what-to-know-about-snap-increases-starting-oct-1-5/)). SNAP expects a family to spend about 30% of its income left after deductions on food. That is roughly $314. So $1,023 − $314 ≈ **$700**.

**What I couldn't confirm**
- I couldn't open USDA's own pages or the official TDHS pages. The exact standard deduction for four people is also not confirmed.
- Tennessee may be changing its income rules. The Sycamore Institute says TDHS is seeking changes ([Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/?p=17208)). You are under the usual limit by a wide margin, so this shouldn't change your result.
- The savings limit is usually **$3,000** for most households, or $4,500 if someone is 60 or older or has a disability ([Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/?p=17208)).

**Next steps**
1. Apply with TDHS. A search pointed to **onedhs.tn.gov**. I couldn't open it, so please confirm it's the official site.
2. Call **211** for free help finding the right phone number or applying.
3. Report your income, rent, and child care costs accurately. If the numbers are wrong, benefits might have to be paid back.

**Two quick questions:**
1. Roughly how much do you have in savings (checking and savings combined)? You don't have to answer.
2. Do you want me to check TennCare or CoverKids for your kids, and WIC? Does anyone in your home have health coverage right now?
$400 or so in checking and savings combined. I don't think any of us has health coverage right now, but I'm not totally sure.

Good news on both counts.

**Food assistance (SNAP):** Your $400 in savings is well under the usual $3,000 limit ([Sycamore Institute](https://sycamoretn.org/?p=17208)). It doesn't change my earlier result. SNAP still looks **likely**, at about $700 a month. That's an estimate.

**Health coverage (TennCare and CoverKids):** I used the state's own chart for a household of 4. I counted your $1,500 pay and your husband's $550 as about $2,050 a month before taxes ([TennCare Eligibility Reference Guide](https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html)).

| Who | Monthly limit | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Your 8-year-old (TennCare) | $3,658 | **Likely** |
| Your 5-year-old (TennCare) | $3,905 | **Likely** |
| Both kids (CoverKids, a backup if TennCare doesn't fit) | $6,875 | **Likely** |
| You and your husband (TennCare for parents) | $2,750 | **Likely**, but this one is closer, so a caseworker will check it |

- The parent limit is the one to watch. Your income is under it, but a caseworker will decide how each income counts.
- One site I found also mentioned a small extra allowance on these limits. I couldn't confirm it, so I didn't count it.
- You said you aren't sure whether anyone has coverage. That's fine. The application will check.

**WIC:** This looks **unlikely** for your family right now. WIC covers children until their fifth birthday, plus pregnant or new moms and babies. Your kids are 5 and 8. I couldn't open the official WIC page, so please confirm this with the Tennessee Department of Health. If someone in your home is pregnant or has a baby, tell me and I'll look again. You can still apply.

**Next steps**
1. **Health coverage:** Apply through TennCare Connect at **855-259-0701**, or use the "How Do I Apply for TennCare?" page at tn.gov/tenncare ([CoverKids page](https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html)). One application can check TennCare and CoverKids.
2. **Food assistance:** Apply with the Tennessee Department of Human Services (TDHS). A search pointed to onedhs.tn.gov, but I couldn't open it, so please confirm it's the official site.
3. **Free local help:** Call **211**.

Please report your income, rent, and child care costs accurately. Only TDHS and TennCare decide who gets help, and my numbers are estimates.

The FY 2027 SNAP adjustments took effect October 1, 2026, and USDA's own memo is the primary source.

- **Effective dates and scope:** USDA's August 21, 2026 memo sets the adjustments for the 48 contiguous states, D.C., Alaska, Guam, Hawaii, and the U.S. Virgin Islands ([USDA memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)). The income standards run from October 1, 2026 through September 30, 2027.
- **Maximum allotments:** The family-of-four maximum in the 48 states and D.C. is $1,023 ([USDA memo](https://www.usda.gov/sites/default/files/guidance-documents/fna.snap-cola2027.pdf)). Hawaii's family-of-four maximum falls to $1,655 ([News4Jax](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)). Alaska's family-of-four range is $1,306 to $2,027 ([Newsweek](https://www.newsweek.com/snap-benefits-are-increasing-october-1-new-payment-amounts-revealed-12393704)). The minimum benefit for one- and two-person households rises to $25 ([Cronista](https://www.cronista.com/en/finance/snap-benefits-increase-starting-october-1-2026-new-maximum-amounts-by-household-size/)).
- **Income standards:** Gross monthly limits for the 48 states and D.C. are $1,729 for one person and $3,575 for a family of four, up from $1,696 and $3,483 ([Colorado Politics](https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/09/28/what-to-know-about-snap-increases-starting-oct-1-5/)). Net monthly limits are $1,330 for one person and $2,750 for four ([Colorado Politics](https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/09/28/what-to-know-about-snap-increases-starting-oct-1-5/)). The elderly and disabled standard is 165% of poverty for households that qualify as separate ([News4Jax](https://www.news4jax.com/news/local/2026/10/02/snap-benefits-increase-for-millions-of-americans/)).
- **Deductions:** The standard deduction for one to three people rises from $209 to $217. The maximum excess shelter deduction rises from $744 to $796 ([Colorado Politics](https://www.coloradopolitics.com/2026/09/28/what-to-know-about-snap-increases-starting-oct-1-5/)).

Sources agree on the figures I checked. The Cronista and Propel pieces list the full maximum-allotment table by household size, which I did not verify against the USDA attachment, since the search returned only the first page of the memo. Use the USDA memo for the complete tables.

Links: [{"title":"Eligibility Reference Guide","url":"https://www.tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility-reference-guide.html"},{"title":"tn.gov","url":"https://tn.gov/content/dam/tn/tenncare/documents/CaretakerRelativeMAGI.pdf"},{"title":"Eligibility Reference Guide","url":"https://www.tn.gov/coverkids/coverkids/redirect-income-guidelines.html"},{"title":"medicaid eligibility tennessee","url":"https://sycamoretn.org/medicaid-eligibility-tennessee/"},{"title":"sycamoretn.org","url":"https://sycamoretn.org/?p=3113"},{"title":"Medicaid eligibility in Tennessee — income limits for 2025","url":"https://www.blackhealth.org/medicaid/tennessee/eligibility/"},{"title":"Eligibility and enrollment in Tennessee Medicaid","url":"https://www.wellpoint.com/tn/medicaid/eligibility-and-enrollment"},{"title":"tn.gov","url":"https://tn.gov/tenncare/members-applicants/eligibility/categories.html"},{"title":"Medicaid in Tennessee: who qualifies and income limits for 2026","url":"https://www.talktomira.com/coverage/medicaid/tennessee/"}]

Tennessee has not expanded Medicaid, so the parent and caretaker relative category has a fixed income cap, and the published figures vary by source and year.

- **Who qualifies:** TennCare's caretaker category covers parents and relatives raising a dependent child under 18, or under 19 if the child is a full-time student. Benefits go to these parents and caretakers whose household income is at or below the standard for their household size. The category has no resource limit. The Caretaker Relative category has a 100% of the poverty level income limit and no resource limit.
- **Dollar limits (2026):** The most recent source, checked against state sources on October 13, 2026, gives monthly limits of $1,397 for one person, $1,894 for two, $2,391 for three, $2,888 for four, $3,385 for five, and $3,882 for six. It says these include the 5% income disregard, so they run 5 points above the percentages Tennessee prints on its own chart.
- **Conflicting figures:** A 2025 source lists the parent limit as 95% FPL, with $24,530 annually for a household of three. The state's own chart, as reproduced in the reference guide, shows 100% FPL. The gap appears to be the 5% disregard, but I did not confirm that against the state's current chart, so check TennCare directly before relying on any single number.
- **Adults without children:** These adults generally can't qualify at any income. Coverage is available only if the person is pregnant, 65 or older, blind, disabled, or a former foster youth under 26. Parents with incomes above the cap but below the poverty line fall into a coverage gap, which one source estimates at too much for Medicaid, too little for ACA marketplace subsidies.

Tennessee WIC serves children from birth up to age 5, along with pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women. Children qualify if they meet the income and residency rules and a health professional finds them at nutritional or medical risk.

- **Age:** The Tennessee Department of Health's program page describes assistance for income-eligible children until their fifth birthday (The Tennessee WIC Program provides supplemental food assistance and nutrition education to income-eligible pregnant, postpartum, and breastfeeding women, infants, and children until age five.). A Kid Central TN listing puts the range at a child Birth to 5 years of age.
- **Income:** The gross household income limit is 185% of the federal poverty level (Have a household gross income at or below 185% of federal poverty). One Tennessee source gives about $55,000 for a family of four as of July 1, though that figure may be outdated and should be checked against current guidelines (As of July 1, approximately $55,000 for a family of 4).
- **Residency:** Applicants must live in Tennessee, though they generally use the county where they live (Can reside anywhere in Tennessee, although it is customary to participate in the county of residence).
- **Nutritional risk:** A health professional must determine that the child has a nutritional or medical risk (applicants must be determined to be at "nutritional risk" by a health professional.).
- **Automatic eligibility:** Children in households receiving SNAP, Families First/TANF, or TennCare are automatically eligible for WIC (Women and children who are already participating in SNAP, Families First/TANF or Tennessee Medicaid (TennCare) programs, are automatically eligible for the WIC program.).
- **Caregivers:** Knox County's FAQ says caregivers who have children under age five who are income eligible may apply, including fathers, grandparents, foster parents, stepparents, and legal guardians. That detail comes from a single county source, so confirm it with the state.

Sources differ slightly on the exact details, so the official Tennessee WIC page at tn.gov/health is the best place to confirm current income limits and how to apply.
